newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Mideast suffering sharp investment drop-U.N..
newsitem.headline: Mideast suffering sharp investment drop-U.N..

text.p: Foreign direct investment (FDI) in the mainly Arab countries of the Middle East has declined from near ten percent of world totals in the early 1980s to less than one per cent, a United Nations report said on Tuesday.

The report, by the world body's Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) said Saudi Arabia -- by far the region's biggest FDI recipient -- was largely responsible for the drop because outside investment in its oil industry had nose-dived.

According to UNCTAD, the decline reflected a softening foreign investor interest in oil and oil-related industries, and a change of focus towards other activities, especially manufacturing and services.

The report said that at the start of the 1980s, the eight major oil-producing and exporting economies among the 15 states of the region which is designated by UNCTAD as West Asia accounted for over 96 percent of total inflows.

By the late 1980s, this declined to around 67 percent, and by the mid-1990s FDI flows to the region were almost equally distributed between the big oil-producers and its seven non-oil states, the U.N. agency said.

Flows to these economies -- who include non-Arab Israel and Cyprus as well as Jordan, Lebanon, areas controlled by the Palestinian Authority, Syria and Yemen -- were now growing faster than to the oil states.

From 1986-90, the report said, the eight oil producers and exporters -- Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- were together receiving an annual average total of $673 million.
The non-producers average over the same period was $327 million.

But in the period 1991-95, although the oil producers were receiving an average of $1,04 billion, an increase of some 54 per cent, the non-producers' average had climbed to $604 million, an improvement of 85 per cent.
During the oil boom of the first half of the 1980s, according to UNCTAD, annual average FDI flows into Saudi Arabia which went almost exclusively into the petroleum industry were some $5 billion.
By 1990-95, they had dropped to just under $737 million.
Although investment in petroleum in the mid-1990s still accounted for the overwhelming share of all FDI in the oil-producing and exporting states, it was still declining.
Oman, UNCTAD said, saw more than 95 per cent of all outside investment going into its petroleum industry at the start of the current decade, but the figure had now dropped to 84 per cent.

Israel, which in the first half of the 1980s was averaging only $76 million of FDI annually, was attracting just under $420 million a year between 1991 and 1995, the report said, becoming the region's second-largest recipient.
Half of the flows were directed into its mechanical and electronic goods industries.
Oman, the third largest recipient with an annual average of $123 million during the 1991-95 period, was also running below its 1980-85 average of $136 million.
But the UAE, receiving only $28 million in 1980-85, hit an annual average of $112 million in the first half of the 1990s.
Cyprus advanced from around $70 million throughout the 1980s to $94 million in the first half of the 1990s, according to UNCTAD.
